utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to all. Yes, I can and I do understand everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner, Timothy Resch and Denise Gustin case manager. Your Honour, may I put in a plea? We have gone from one extreme to another, it's from freezing to excessive heat and I don't want the temperature of Mr. Ackerman's cross-examination to be raised. Alternatively nor do I wish to go to sleep because of the heat. I wonder if there is anything we can do to get this turned down. It's unbearable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you Ms. Korner, I was going to ask --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because you could feel it the moment you walk in. Thank you, Ms. Korner and good morning to you all. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours I'm John Ackerman. I'm with Milan Trbojevic and Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you all. Let's bring the witness in. In the meantime or by the time he comes in, any filings, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour with regard to the Rule 92 bis, I've explained to the Prosecutor that I can't do anything with them until they give me the witness list which they still have not done. I have to know who the witnesses are before I can determine whether there is duplication and things of that nature. I cannot respond until I get those. I think I'll get them today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't understand how Mr. Ackerman can say that as not a minute ago, he and Ms. Jevtovic had a discussion putting it politely about the witnesses that were coming so -- but we need to know about Donji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have the witness list. They haven't been given to me. I have a schedule of the witnesses that will be appearing the week of the 24th but I don't have the witness lists for Donji Vakuf and Prnjavor. I have not been given them. I asked for them yesterday. I still don't have them although I'm told that they have been printed and they will be given to me today. That's where it stands and if I was just given them this morning I have not had time this morning yet to do the filing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You deal with it during the first break, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome back. Could we go through the same routine again, please? We ask you to repeat your solemn undertaking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please be seated. And Mr. Ackerman will proceed with his cross-examination. Thank you. Yes. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are you okay today?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good. Me too. I just want to deal with a couple of little things and then go back to where we left off yesterday. I want to just ask you this question sort of globally about your entire experience in former Yugoslavia, 1992, 1993, 1994, 1995, through that period. You made the observation at one point that from that experience, that one of the things you learned that frequently the person that you needed to deal with, who actually had the power and authority to respond to some of your needs was not necessarily the person who had the title. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: With due respect, I am not sure I recall anything to that language. Maybe you can be specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me, during the break I'll see if I can find the exact language. I can't find it for you right at this moment but I'll try to find it during the break and be more specific with you, thank you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We talked a bit yesterday about -- at the very beginning of your testimony, about the conditions in Bosnia in 1992. And it's page 73, line 4 of your testimony yesterday. You said this, you were talking about speaking to mayors and other people located in your sector. You spoke of -- let me see if I can get the -- you were talking about the military situation and how you believe that there were signs that Banja Luka was exercising a balance of military power over Knin and you explained what caused you to arrive at that, and you went on in more questions were asked about that and finally, the question was: You say they had a tendency to retreat to Banja Luka to do what or to Belgrade and then you gave this answer: You have to think again I was speaking about mayors and other people located in the sector, they were surrounded on the confrontation line by the Croats in the direction of Karlovac, Sisak and Zagreb. Another way of putting it too, they were also blockaded themselves. We didn't mention that. The Serbs were blockaded in that sense. Economically they can't go out, they couldn't get their fuel out, and then there is some word that I can't read, S-P-O-E-S-H-G-S whatever that is, they couldn't get most normal things because of the war, the electricity was not working because things had been broken up, broken down, and with the political, the grid, electrical grid, normal things weren't working, like water, because there were no pumps so in a way there was a situation of shortages even for the Serbs. So for them to redress that they had to get out somehow and that's the corridor that took them to Banja Luka or Belgrade for the purpose of redressing shortages in normal every day economic life. That was the case, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, I want to go back to DB134 and DB135, please. I'll ask you be handed both of those documents. Now, let me see if I can make it easier for you and I to communicate about these documents because I think we had some difficulty yesterday. What I'm interested in with regard to these documents is first of all that they were documents that were in existence prior to your arrival in former Yugoslavia, that you had access to. The two questions I have are this: Do you recall ever reading the documents? And whether or not do you recall having been privy to the information contained in these documents at some time around the time that you arrived in former Yugoslavia? We are down to about halfway through that situation on the ground paragraph 8 paragraph that we were discussing yesterday. The next sentence, and I think it's fair, first of all, to just confirm with you that this paragraph is talking about the current situation in regard to Yugoslavia, that being the entire former Yugoslavia at that point?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour he said he was going to ask two questions and then went on. I think the answer to the two questions ought to come first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't know that I really asked any.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First, had he ever read them and whether or not he would be privy to the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going to do that. No, I'm going to do that. I'm just telling him up front how I'm going to proceed. That wasn't a question. That was just direction as to how I'm going to proceed with all of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understood you the same way Ms. Korner did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm glad I went through that effort to try to make things clearer so everybody could understand what I was trying to do. It was really successful. I guess I'll have to try again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a number of questions about these documents, sir. And in each instance, all I'm referring to is documents that were available to you before April of 1992, when you went there, and whether or not you either became aware of what was in the document in some other way or whether you actually read the information that was in the document. And I will deal with that with each issue that I discuss with you. And I'm now about halfway through paragraph 8, A, situation on the ground. The next sentence is: Ports and military facilities have been blockaded, air space has been closed, communications severely disrupted. Now, bearing in mind what I just explained, one, had you read this before you went there, two, were you aware of it at about the time you did get there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have a general comment to make. Just as he prepared his own questions, I'm going to prepare my own answers. The context. Your Honour, I drew your attention to these reports' date. The date, 25th of October, 1991. Nothing in the testimony I've given to you, this Court, covers any of that period. The testimony I've given to this Court covers April, 1992 and, if Ms. Korner can check, probably up to August, 1992. Nothing, I repeat, nothing in the testimony I've given covers anything else except that period. Second point, reports of the Secretary-General are many and are prepared by a lot of people and one of the things you should know delegates in the UN complain is the multitude of those documents. They are plenty. Therefore, for counsellor to ask me whether I was aware of reports of the Secretary-General or read any specific one, in general my answer will be, whether I read them or didn't read them, I have no information to add about the content of that report having not participated in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, now having given that explanation, I'd like you to answer my question. Do you recall reading this report? If not, were you aware of the information contained within the sentence that I read to you at or about the time you arrived in former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer to your question is already given to you in my earlier statement. I did not have any direct involvement in this report. Or having read it, I can read it now and tell you yes, I'm aware now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, with all due respect you're not answering my question. Let me put it in a different way. Ports and military facilities have been blockaded, air space has been closed and communications severely disrupted. Were you aware at or about April of 1992, that that was the situation in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no. The question is -- well actually what Mr. Ackerman is trying to find out from the witness is how much information related to the substance of that report, irrespective of whether he had read it or not, was in Mr. Kirudja's possession at the time of his arrival.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour that's right, but I think the question -- it's not clear, I don't think, and maybe not to the witness, was he aware that in 1991 this was the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But let him answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's not my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What happened in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What happened in 1991 need not have been continuing in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry I don't want to waste time and I appreciate Mr. Ackerman wants to finish but the question actually reads, ports and military facilities have been blockaded, air space has been closed and communications severely disrupted. That was in October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Pre-October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: October -- exactly. The question then was were you aware of this? When was he aware this is what the situation was in 1991 or is it suggested the same situation pertained in April, 1992? That I think is the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The question Your Honour is just simple. Were you aware at or about April 1992 that that was the situation in Yugoslavia? I'm not talking about 1991. I'm talking about April, 1992, when he got there. Did that situation persist when he arrived there? Was he aware of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is easy to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I keep getting interrupted by Ms. Korner and everybody else. I think the questions are clear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour the last question is easy for me to answer. In April, 1992, I was travelling through Belgrade and I wasn't aware of the ports or the situation of the ports in Yugoslavia. I was on travel status.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the rest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, did the situation persist?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Air space was closed communications severely disrupted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Military facilities blockaded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Wasn't aware of that. The airport was open. We landed in Belgrade and everything seemed normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There have moreover been forced evacuations of large and growing numbers of civilians from their homes, suggesting the existence of a desire in some quarters to alter the demographic composition of certain areas with a view to holding territorial advantage later on. The civilian population in effected areas has by the same token suffered and continues to suffer a tragically high rate of casualties despite numerous declared cease-fires. When you arrived in the area in 1992, were you aware of that situation persisting at that time?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of the situation. I could see in the areas I passed through in April. I passed through parts of Yugoslavia through Belgrade into Sector East. I was aware of the war that had ravaged those areas. I could see it. And I could see the difficulties in each of the areas I passed through.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Look now at the -- at page 458 of this document, under heading, B, humanitarian situation, paragraph 15 reads as follows: "The unabated fighting, especially in eastern Croatia and on the Dalmatian coast has gravely disrupted the living conditions of the civilian population in these areas. The most serious humanitarian problem caused by the fighting, aside from direct casualties and the destruction of housing, and various --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is the alarming growth in the number of displaced persons within Yugoslavia. Present indications are that the total number of internally displaced persons is approximately 300.000. While according to the most recent estimates of ICRC that number is capable of increasing to at least 400.000 towards the end of 1991. Observers on the ground expect that in the coming weeks, the number of forcibly displaced persons primarily those moving from the Dalmatian coast -- east coast towards the north and from the crisis areas in eastern Croatia will increase significantly if a lasting cease-fire does not take effect. Were you aware, at any time, after your arrival, or before, in former Yugoslavia, of this -- these large numbers of displaced persons resulting from the war in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The evidence of displaced persons became hard not to see as one got into the areas where the mission was deployed, where we were supposed to be deployed. It was plainly evident in parts of Croatia where the mission was to be deployed, there were displacements of people. The destruction of houses, and generally the tell tales of the ravages of war just completed or for which the cease-fire had been obtained prior to our arrival. That was evident.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Paragraph 17, thank you. As regards refugees who have fled Yugoslavia to other countries, the growing number leaving the battle areas, in particular the Slavonia region in eastern Croatia is a matter of particular concern. At the request of the government of Hungary, the office of the United Nations high commissioner for refugees is already in the process of bringing assistance to refugees who have been arriving in Hungary from Yugoslavia and who at present number some 35.000 persons. Italy has granted temporary asylum status to 5.000 Yugoslavs. Austria has reported that it has granted temporary asylum to 6.000 to 8.000 persons from Slovenia. Were you aware of these rough numbers of persons who had become refugees in other countries in the area?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not directly about refugees in those localities or in the numbers you cited. I was aware of the areas that many displaced people had come from. That I could see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were you aware that large numbers of these displaced persons and refugees were Serbs being expelled from areas of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on, it was easy for me to piece together particularly in the sector where I was deployed, the kind of ethnicities of the people who were displaced. It was easy to -- later -- on location, to look at the displaced areas and talking to the people inside, I was aware of what kind of people had been displaced from any of those places where we were deployed -- deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the answer is?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is, it differed. For example in Sector North, municipality by municipality, there were both Croats and Serbs displaced, but in different directions. If, for example, to give you an example, if you look at the area we discussed yesterday, bordering Bosnia and Herzegovina, the displaced people were Serbs inside my sector coming from different parts across the border. In certain opstinas, the displaced people were Croats who used to be in those areas and who were displaced across the confrontation line in the -- to the areas where the Croat authorities had -- where the Croat government had authority as opposed to the area where we were deployed where they didn't. Therefore, it was always specific and in directions. There were Serbs, there were Croats, there were Muslims, displaced.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May we remind the speakers to pause between question and answer? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The next paragraph I want to refer you to is paragraph 19, talking about economic aspects. Yugoslavia's economy had already been experiencing considerable difficulty prior to the outbreak of hostilities, owing to demands of an ambitious stabilisation programme being pursued in the context of an evaporating federal consensus. The growing hostilities have exacerbated the problems and the economy is, as a result, now in a rapid downward spiral. Production in all sectors has fallen off dramatically. Fiscal policy has collapsed. Inflation has accelerated greatly. The financial system has split apart. The infrastructure of communications has been severely disrupted and trade and remittances from overseas have declined precipitously. Were you personally able to observe any of those economic problems that were existing in Yugoslavia at or about that time?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the areas where we were deployed, we not only were aware of it but we also set out to address some of those infrastructural deficiencies, a point I alluded to when I asked what were part of my responsibilities. We were aware and we saw the need to help a lot of -- to help with the situation we found in the areas where we were deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go now to the next document. That would be DB135. And I think we can deal with this very briefly. I'm only interested in page 475, paragraph 15 of that document. Now, this document is a later report dated 11 December, 1991. Paragraph 15 is dealing with the humanitarian aspects of what was going on in Yugoslavia at that time. And again this is a Secretary-General's report. He says, "The humanitarian dimensions of the Yugoslavia problem on which I dwelt at some length in my report of 25 October, 1991, have continued to grow. The number of persons displaced by the conflict now exceeds 500.000 and is increasing still. Two-thirds of the displaced persons are women and children. Indigenous resources for assistance to this population are rapidly being depleted, and the local hospitality which today has permitted the placement of well over half of the displaced persons with host families is eroding. The ever-more difficult economic situation, shortages, the high cost of certain basic household items and of fuel, as well as rising unemployment and the onset of winter are likely to compel even more displaced persons to seek shelter in collective facilities. Although most of the displaced remain within the frontiers of Yugoslavia's six republics, a growing number have sought refuge in other countries, in particular in Hungary which now hosts over 40.000 persons. That, sir, is just kind of an update on what we had read previously about that, and to your knowledge, that's -- that's what was happening, correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the report states.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, considering the kind of situation in Yugoslavia that these reports from as early as late 1991, describe, it wouldn't be unusual for one caught up in the middle of that situation, who has relatives or friends in Austria or Germany, inviting them to come there, voluntarily being willing to leave this rather horrid situation in Yugoslavia and go to the relative safety and economic security of some Western country would it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a general question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wouldn't be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this situation that the Secretary-General describes with regard to the displacement of people, the growing refugee problem and the severe economic problems, does not sound like a situation one would describe as people living in the comfort of their homes, does it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, Mr. Ackerman, that reference of people living in your home is a specific reference to a time and place. What you read, and I answered, is general. That's a truism. It doesn't follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, yes. I understand you want to restrict that to a specific time and place, and I understand you want to keep not talking about the word "comfort" because it's your word but actually what you talked about was people leaving the comfort of their homes, and the specific time and place was in early 1992, in Bosanski Novi, which was in Yugoslavia, in this place where all these economic problems were occurring throughout the country, and in this place where war was going on and in this --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry can I stop this speech now, please? What's the actual question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm asking the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, it sounds like a speech to me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him finish. I can see the question actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That was an effective interruption, Your Honour. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I've lost my train.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Maybe you can start it again. I can read it out for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is Your Honour ruling that that is a proper question as opposed to a speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He is confronting the witness with all these facts, as running counter to the whole concept of comfort of one's home. You can't, in other words, enjoy the comforts of your own home in the circumstances that he has quoted the report depicts. This is the question. I mean it's -- it's true that he's making a speech but the question is there. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, at this specific time and place that you want to refer to in Bosanski Novi in 1992, Bosanski Novi was located within this Yugoslavia that was experiencing all of these economic difficulties and all of these displacements of persons, and do you still want to maintain that people were living in Bosanski Novi in these horrid situations in the comfort of their homes?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, let me remind you what I said. You are now saying it was a statement that people were living in the comfort of their home. If you look at the record, it was a question asked of me to the mayor. It's not a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, what it was, sir, was this: You said that you could not accept that these people wanted to leave there voluntarily because they were living in the comfort of their homes and people living in the comfort of their homes do not want to leave a place voluntarily. Now, that was your conclusion based upon what you were told about whether or not they were leaving voluntarily. You drew the conclusion that that was a sham. And all I'm suggesting to you is it's perfectly natural that people in the situation that existed in former Yugoslavia at that time, given the opportunity, would go somewhere else where they were safe and comfortable, that there was no comfort in their homes at that time. Now that's what I'm suggesting to you.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can suggest that. It does not change my testimony. You can suggest, you can rationalise it. If you look at the testimony, the sequence was this: I get a mayor. He comes to my office and he says to me, "We got a report, I've been told by my colleague third hand".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you. You've made your point quite clear. You don't need to repeat it, Mr. Kirudja. Let's move forward, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going forward, Your Honour, to that first contact Mr. Kirudja, that you had with -- I believe it was the mayor of Novi?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The mayor of Dvor?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Talking about these 5.000 people wanting to have safe conduct across Sector North, and there were two -- two things that were really requested, safe conduct and as we mentioned yesterday that you would provide an international television crew to cover that process?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: With an international television crew there, wouldn't that really make for a golden opportunity for these 5.000 refugees, if they were being banished rather than leaving voluntarily, to go on international television and make that clear to the world?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point, I put that aside temporarily. At that point, my testimony indicates I wanted to hear from them themselves, that I ascertain this wish directly from them. So at that meeting, I put that request aside.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But isn't it the case that the willingness of the people in Bosanski Novi, the authorities in Bosanski Novi, apparently, to have this whole process photographed by international television, would have been an opportunity for those people, if they were not leaving voluntarily, to make that clear?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they were telling me themselves that, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to ask you about this person, Paolo Raffone. Is that how you say his name?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correctly, very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Not too bad, huh?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Was he a reliable person would you say during the time he worked for you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you find his reports to be basically accurate?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ones I cleared as you can see are released under my signature, I did find them accurate enough for me to release them. And when I say that, there may be figures here where he didn't get right the number of refugees there. If you mean by accurate, did he count and tally, there are -- there are even in my own testimony times where the numbers don't tally. If he is reporting to me on issues that I check out, he was generally correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think, sir that sometimes you're anticipating where I might be going and thereby answering a question in much more detail than necessary. Let's try not to do that so we can finish today?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I will be until of course when you asked me was he being accurate that's a blanket statement. I have to tell you in what sense I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You answer him generally and in a blanket statement too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Look at P1661, please. Now, P1661, sir, is a memorandum written by Mr. Raffone, and then released by you with your signature, correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what is reported in that memorandum is that Mr. Raffone said that on 1 June, 1992, he got a call from Mr. Kupresanin, the mayor of Banja Luka, correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the paragraph on the top says, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever question whether it was the case that Mr. Kupresanin was the mayor of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was -- he wasn't meeting him directly so I didn't question him. I questioned him how he got that information, the information was on the telephone, through an interpreter. The interpreter interpreted him as saying, "I am the mayor." That's what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now the question I asked you I think was quite simple: Did you ever question whether it was the case that Mr. Kupresanin was the mayor of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's try to do that. Let's try to answer them that way unless you absolutely need to explain something. Did you ever learn differently, other than what's reported here, that Mr. Kupresanin was the mayor of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How long afterward did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall how long but after -- after speaking with him, said no, the name Kupresanin is itself indicative of the names that we wanted to clarify so we were already -- we were always changing titles of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you say that from reading the report, from this reliable person, Mr. Raffone, that one thing that's certain is that he did have a conversation with Mr. Kupresanin on 1 June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And would you also say that at the time he had that conversation, he believed that Mr. Kupresanin was the mayor of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the presentation he was given to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your testimony yesterday, page 19, line 9, you were asked about Banja Luka in connection with this July memo found in document P1671. So I'll ask that you look at that, please. At page 19 of yesterday's testimony, you were asked by Ms. Korner this question. Now, I'm referring to this document 1671, which if you'll notice in the second paragraph contains the name Banja Luka. You were asked how that came into it and you said that Banja Luka found its way into that memorandum, and this is your answer, this you will recall there was a telephone call received by Mr. Paolo Raffone where Mr. Kupresanin had also alluded to the same towns and warning from his own count 15.000 people had left the area of Banja Luka and warning that 15.000 more would follow, and then saying to us, please, the international organisation, we need the assistance of the humanitarian agencies in this crisis. Sir that was the answer you gave us yesterday, was it not?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you know that that's not a true answer, don't you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You know that it's not true?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you not? I'm telling you. You know that it's not true, don't you, that Mr. Kupresanin said that 15.000 people had left the area of Banja Luka and 15.000 more would follow?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We reported what -- I don't understand what is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You said in your testimony yesterday that Mr. Kupresanin had said that 15.000 people had left the area of Banja Luka and 15.000 more were coming.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is testimony to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What I'm saying to you, you know that that's not true, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But who was supposed to -- Mr. Ackerman, who is supposed to have said that untruth? Mr. Kupresanin or the person who is drafting this report?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think he's suggesting that Mr. Kirudja is telling an untruth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I would like to know what that's based on too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm coming to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja actually was referring to what is written in the report. He couldn't have been saying an untruth himself, if there is an untruth in that statement, the untruth is contained in the report, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman at the moment it's my understanding and he's just confirmed it is suggesting that Mr. Kirudja is deliberately lying when he says that is what he was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then perhaps you'd like to make it clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What I'm suggesting is that what Mr. Kirudja said about that yesterday in answer to this question that 15.000 people left the area of Banja Luka and 15.000 more would follow was a misstatement, and probably an unintentional one, of the actual facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And now I will ask you, sir, about the actual facts and see if you agree with me. If you look at P1661, again, please, this is the document that talks about the phone call from Mr. Kupresanin. The end of that first paragraph says the mayor's information can be summarised as follows.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the report you're quoting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you just had it a moment ago. What happened to it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't see that. What is the reference of P what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: P1661, Mr. Kirudja, first part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Under A, phone call from the mayor of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go right to the end of that part, first part, A, and it's the penultimate paragraph. The mayor estimates that some 15.000 persons have already left the normal place of residence moving towards Dvor and some more 15.000 might follow in a short time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Actually I want to take you up to the end of the first paragraph under A, the last sentence says the mayor's information can be summarised as followings. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then you see the mayors of Bosanski Novi, Prijedor, Kljuc, Dubica, Sanski Most, and the one in Banja Luka had contacts about the situation of the Muslim population in the area?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In other words, they had apparently spoken to each other?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And based upon that conversation, based upon that information, Mr. Kupresanin then reported that 15.000 persons have already left their normal place of residence moving towards Dvor and 15.000 more might follow.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What he's saying, according to this report, is that includes refugees from Bosanski Novi, Prijedor, Kljuc, Dubica, Sanski Most and perhaps Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, can you go to my paragraph, the one you quoted me, and see why that is not true? And tell me why it isn't true?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, it would be true if the area of Banja Luka included all of these places. Is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please read it aloud again. I'll tell you what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Kupresanin alluded to the same towns and warning from him --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stop there a minute, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: M'hm?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Alluded to the same towns, that's the reference to the towns you read on paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And warning from his own count, 15.000 people had left the area of Banja Luka and warning that 15.000 more would follow.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the reference to the paragraph at the bottom. Now, sir, I ask you: What was not true? And you said I knew wasn't true?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you include all of these towns were in the area of Banja Luka, then I will accept that you were telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment, Mr. Ackerman and Mr. Kirudja, you're creating a little bit of a problem to the French interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, and apology to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please slow down and allow a pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you include all these other municipalities in that phrase, area of Banja Luka, then I accept that your statement was accurate. Do you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you also accept that you didn't understand my statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Kirudja, you are not being treated as a hostile witness. No one considers you as a hostile witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You belong to the Court. You are a witness of this Court. Please don't treat Mr. Ackerman as if he is in confrontation with you. He's doing his duty here. He's asking you questions. Try to answer those questions concisely, to the point, so let's get over and done with.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because otherwise, I see that you are very keen, both of you, in --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the greatest of respect, Mr. Ackerman, much as he tries to, is suggesting that this witness has deliberately misled the Court but the witness is entitled to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But in a courteous manner which does not sound confrontational. It was something that he could answer without -- without being confrontational. The thing is that you can feel the confrontation building up and it started yesterday, and I want to avoid it. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, let's see if you can answer my question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, I mean what I have just said to Mr. Kirudja I say to you because you could easily, easily fronted the witness without alleging that he was telling an untruth, that he was not being accurate, because that would have reflected the position, the situation much, much better. And avoided the confrontation that has been building up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you accept, sir, that when you said 15.000 people left the area of Banja Luka, that that includes all these other towns, then I accept that your statement was accurate. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because my reading of this communication that we have talked about, where Mr. Kupresanin is talking about his estimates of 15.000 persons -- their normal place plus the other, this is what he is telling us and I'm reporting it without changing what or rather our report is reflecting without changing Mr. Kupresanin's estimates. We have testified in other information that would not tally with the conclusion you're making.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I mean I don't want to pursue this either but I would like Mr. Ackerman to point out to the Court why those 15.000 people definitely refer back to Novi, Prijedor, Kljuc, Dubica, Sanski Most. That's what he's asserting. I would like to know the basis from this document of that assertion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's next. I'm doing my best here. I'm getting a lot of interruptions. That's next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead but please take the points made by Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm in the middle of this, not the end of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought you would be. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Frankly I think these interruptions are intentional to break up my cross-examination and I'm getting tired of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, you testified on 3 February, 2003, in the Milosevic case. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did testify in that case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going to read to you some questions and answers you gave there. Page 15434. Question: Mr. Kirudja I want to draw your attention now to some other areas, different than Bosanski Novi and ask you some specific questions about them and the areas I want to draw your attention to now are Prijedor, Bosanski Novi, Kljuc, Dubica, Sanski Most and Banja Luka. On the 1st of June, 1992, did Mr. Kupresanin the mayor of Banja Luka, make a report or have a conversation with your office regarding the situation of Muslims in those municipalities? Answer: Yes. It was a telephone call received by Mr. Raffone. Question: Please describe what occurred. Answer: This was a telephone call that Raffone took and made note of what he was being told by the mayor of Banja Luka. And the mayor of Banja Luka, the gist of what he told him, was to the effect that there were already 15.000 refugees, already leaving the area in the towns that you have mentioned, namely Bosanski Novi, Sanski Most, Prijedor, Kljuc and Bosanska Dubica, and that there would be 15.000 more to follow, and that he pleaded that United Nations, the UNHCR, these people needed assistance from them. That was the gist of his call. Now, that was your testimony in Milosevic, wasn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like you to look now at document P1666. And while that's coming, you'd agree with me, don't you, that you have no specific knowledge of any refugees coming into your area coming out of Banja Luka, do you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last testimony that we discussed yesterday was a group of refugees coming into our sector. In the cable that was difficult for Your Honours to read. It did refer to a group coming from Trnopolje and if I'm -- if I can get the reference to that, maybe there was a mention of Banja Luka, but in general, most of the refugees came from the towns nearer to the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. This document that you have in front of you now, this document P166, you see it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I -- this is the document with the report of the gentleman from UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There is a note dated 9 June, 1992, has your name on it but someone else signed it for you.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You see that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know who that is that signed it there? Is that Paolo Raffone?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You authorised him to sign this particular document for you, did you not?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And of course you wouldn't consider yourself responsible for such a document absent your having authorised him to sign it for you, would you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a system we follow, when the reports have to be filed by a certain time, and you're not in the office for other reasons, this is the system followed so that he can clear, either by radio or by talking to me and then he would clear, I would say go ahead and put it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And my question is you wouldn't be responsible for such a document absent you having authorised someone to sign it, would you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you saying my authorising it is not responsible or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, no, no. You misunderstood me. Consider the situation where someone had done this without your authorisation?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, it wouldn't be right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you wouldn't be responsible for that document in that situation?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I would have course, if he is my subordinate take issue with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, please find, if you will, your diary entry for 13 June?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There was a meeting went on that day, was there not?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Dvor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And who was in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Deputy mayor of Dvor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Anyone else?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't note my diary did not go further than that to specify in this particular meeting but typically there would have been a civil police -- we have civil police located there, military. There were other people who normally would come into that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Tell the Judges, if you will, what was discussed at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This -- the mayor -- the deputy mayor went straight to the killings of 7 TDF people by Muslims in the area of Dvor. He started by announcing to us there had been seven killings by Muslims. Characterised the situation as provocations by the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He went on to discuss about UNHCR, he said he was glad to have Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. UNPROFOR to hear his claim about these provocations. Several pages of it, about three pages. Do you want me to go through that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I want to know what happened in that meeting. You can do it in a very summary fashion but I would just like to know the basic ...

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said I have three pages of different matters on my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right? He wanted to speed up UNPROFOR deployment in Dvor, expects the conflict to escalate, began to collect weapons in the area, equipment of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, talked about conditions of the opening of the new front that had been fulfilled, this is -- and he went on to say this is a classical aggression of one member of the UN, Muslims have crossed into the RSK and are present. They estimate two battalions of well-armed Muslims. Border is 40 kilometres long. The flash points were in Cazin, Velika Kladusa, Bosanska Krupa, all inhabited by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you a minute. These two battalions of Muslims he was talking about where was it he was saying that these were located?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He said the border is 40 kilometres long and there were flash points.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Before that you talked about two battalions of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no specific locations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He said they are expected.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allowed a number of Muslims to come into the territories. There was a massacre of seven people which took place in Cokovac. They went to Ljubljana and villages in Dvor. At present there are shootings on the border from Letici, Sircic and down to Kekic Klanac. All along the opstina border with Velika Kladusa and Bosanska Krupa. Opstinas in Bosnia-Herzegovina. He allowed Muslims who wanted to -- rather he charged that Muslims who wanted to escape were allowed. They are here now in Dvor. Many others were transported through Krajina into villages in Bosanska Krupa, by cars, from Bosanski Novi. About 30.000 people, able to bear arms and fight, many of them are illiterate and fundamentalist Muslims. One battalion came into the territory in -- intending to attack this opstina. The purpose was to interrupt the UN. Present -- okay. I noted now there was Milan Junic who was the deputy mayor, and present at the committee -- president of the committee of the cooperation with UNPROFOR. There was also Milan Vucjak [phoen] president of the government of Dvor. We went on to discuss the structure of the local government. He told me that there were 270 deputies in the parliament of the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, you can skip the structure of the local government.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then he spoke to me about the UNHCR and said -- no, the UNHCR are -- made their own presentation about displaced persons. I think they made him aware about 500.000 displaced in Croatia and 400.000 in new Yugoslavia. These were figures that UNHCR was talking to the mayor about. And he went on to inform me that local officials have 4.900 refugees, including 1.700 refugees from Zagreb, Sisak and elsewhere in Croatia. They are accommodated by other people and they are -- but they are accommodated by other people and the Red Cross, but they are -- but they came in with nothing. He wanted to inform me about the opstina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: These refugees - excuse me - these refugees you're talking about there -- that he's talking about there would be --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Serb refugees coming out of Croatia into Bosnia or into Novi at least?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Into Dvor?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Into Dvor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, all right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The opstina size, 505 -- 5.505 square kilometres with 15.000 inhabitants before the war. That is Dvor. Add the refugees who came in, 4.900, into Dvor, these are again would be Serb. At one moment up to 6.000 displaced persons. A lot have now returned to towns in the UNPA, meaning Petrinja, Glina and Kostajnica. Then the mayor started to -- went -- resumed from there and began to talk again about the Muslims, have Muslims here that we take care of. Can take -- we can take you to see the families in Dvor. There are also Croats in Dvor. You may speak to them without our presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you accept that invitation and go to speak to the Muslim and Croat families in Dvor?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Remember I'm the head of the UN in that area and I tasked our own civil police to go into the areas where they are, they would go and look.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So the answer is no, you did not?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is someone in my team would. This is internal to the sector and they did go. Their job was to routinely do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are preparing to allow the return -- to allow returnees back to have their villages here. Representatives of ICRC visited Dvor in November. He mentioned someone from ICRC, I don't know whether Your Honour you want me to mention people from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Was later killed in Sarajevo. This ICRC representative. International money was promised for assistance to Serbian Krajina. Money probably went to banks in Belgrade, which he believes would be danger to send the food or something like -- of that kind. He began to speak about the complications of -- due to the embargo. We can live ten years with measures -- he went on to tell us we can live for ten years with these sanctions, the Serb area, that the embargo wouldn't change their views. When UNPROFOR has taken over, we will be entitled to exports and imports. He spoke about the harvest and the need for farm equipment because of shortages of fuel. We are ready to go manual in farming if necessary and we will survive. If UNPROFOR brings fuel, they could monitor to see the fuel is used only for agricultural purposes. They will pay for the fuel with their goods, meaning the Serbs, if we give them the fuel, they will pay with their goods. It is a -- it's a critical problem in these areas, fuel. The last UNHCR assistant to the area of Dvor was in mid-February. I've got a lot if you want to go into all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think that's enough. Thank you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want you to look at and I'll tell the Registrar I'll be using first P1668, then P1665, then P1671. Let's go first with P1668.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May we remind the speakers once again to read slowly the documents and to pause between question and answer? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have P1668 before you, sir?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this the memorandum 16th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In paragraph 4, about halfway through, and I think this refers to what you were just telling us about this meeting you had in Dvor, in the last few days, local authorities in the UNPA have brought to the attention of UNPROFOR sensational killings of 7 TDF members in Dvor and 4 TDF members in Siljkovaca near Velika Kladusa. The latter were part of a convoy reportedly escorting 12 children, 11 women and 37 elderly people, all Serbs, into the UNPA. In Cazin, the local TDF authorities claim Muslims --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't have the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You don't have the second page?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry. It's in the wrong place. I have it. That continues TDF authorities claim Muslims --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Axed 40 Serbians to death in the last two days, correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then it says this. And this is a report written by you. And it says this: None of these stories have been verified by independent sources, correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's what you wrote?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, go down, if you will, then, to paragraph 7. And about halfway through that paragraph, you say this: The SDS president, Mr. Beslas -- and I assume we are still talking about Bihac here, the SDS president Mr. Beslas reportedly prepared a document in consultation with the Serbian authorities in Banja Luka to be forwarded to the Muslim authorities in Bihac. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, do you know whether or not that was independently verified?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The word "reportedly" underscores it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. So any time we see the word "reportedly" or something of that nature, then it has not been independently verified?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. This is something I consciously instructed even my colleagues to allege or report if you can't verify, and if you see that word, it signifies that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So if you go back up to paragraph 4, about halfway through, speaking about these children and women, it says the latter were part of a convoy reportedly escorting 12 children, 11 women, 37 elderly, same use there, reportedly?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Same, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Why did you feel it necessary to then add none of these stories have been verified by independent sources?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To underscore the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It merely underscores the word "reportedly."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would it be the case that it underscores what had become a tendency on your part to disbelieve Serb reports and believe Muslim reports?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it won't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Paragraph 8 of this document, on 14 June, 1992, the TDF commander Kordun informed the sector commander and the CAC and an ultimatum was received from Muslim leaders in the villages of Rojnica and -- is that Bugar, both in Cazin. That's in Bosnia. Telling all Muslims living in Kordun to pick up their stuff and return to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, apparently that is a verified situation because there is no "reportedly" or anything like that there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. CAC is me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And do you have any idea why a -- why Muslim leaders in the Cazin area would be sending an ultimatum to Muslims in Kordun to pick up their stuff and return to Bosnia? Do you have any idea why they would be doing that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a very condensed story in that paragraph, Mr. Ackerman, and in this case, if the Court permits, we can tell you the background, because it's not in the direction you may be thinking. These are Muslims inside Kordun, in the sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Before we go any further, let's do this. Look at P1645, will you? We will put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 45, it's that large map, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We'll put this on the ELMO, sir and just show the Judges this area that you're referring to when you speak of Kordun.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This map is not sufficient, but only approximate. The middle, this is the international border we have spoken so many times about. The Kordun area would be somewhere roughly from here, this whole area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir if you look there between Karlovac and the border you'll actually see the word "Kordun" written there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you wouldn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, you will.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You'll see a big one -- Kordun.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There you go?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a town, a region.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So Kordun was a region, not a town?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a town.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. So when you speak of Muslims living in Kordun, you're speaking of Muslims living in that --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Living insides this area, somewhere very close to this border, and they one day, the commanders come and tell me, "We have received an ultimatum that they should leave, like they were being reclaimed back in the bigger area of the Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You mentioned at some point that Muslims were living quietly in the Kordun area.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That particular village, those towns, there were quietly meaning peacefully. It's another way of saying without any harassment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, go ahead and tell us your understanding of the purpose of this ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Eventually, the -- it prepared the ground for us to have these people transferred from Kordun into the Bihac pocket, eventually.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Why would the -- why would the Muslim authorities be issuing an ultimatum to these people to drop everything and come back?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now you are speaking like me now talking to Kordun. That's the kind of question I would have asked -- I asked them, if we were to go into the details, similar to the question I was asking the mayor of Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What kind of an answer did you get?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the full details of what the answer. And back again it also carried now, normally in the fact that I was frequently on the other side of Bihac pocket in Velika Kladusa and Bihac. The Muslims, as you have seen in other reports, had no trouble talking to me directly, and in this case, the matter is being relayed to me through the TDF commander. So it carried the reason for me to make the same questions you're asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So the answer is you don't know?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is that in the end, we knew that trouble was coming and in the end those Muslims were moved across.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were these people who were refugees in the Kordun area or is that their home?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was their home.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Let's go to -- now, to -- we can stop with the map. We can go to P1671. And sir, this is the document that you talked about at length yesterday that I think you said became a rather controversial document.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The first thing that this document reveals, of course, is that at least by 3 July, 1992, you had some information about the existence of camps in Keraterm, Trnopolje, Omarska and Manjaca, correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have any -- any ability, as you sit here today, to tell us how long before that date of 3 July you became aware of these places?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can't give you the exact date but you have phrased it quite accurately, by this date, that we had that awareness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I notice up in the upper right-hand corner of the first page of this document, the words "restricted." Could you tell the Judges what that means in UN language? What does "restricted" mean?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A very good point. The reports of this nature were to be distinguished from a sit-rep or others, but in the system you did have to indicate to who this report was addressed, and the facts that you didn't intend it to be a public document. That would be distributed to everybody. We have 38.000 members of the force. It wouldn't be that kind of document. So restricted meant to the persons addressed and to the person it was copied to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So in this case, it would have gone to Ms. Auger?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And to Mr. Magnusson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And to Mr. Magnusson?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How would it have gotten then if you restricted it to those two, did they have that authority to distribute it further if they wanted to?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Often, since I addressed to a person who will track me it stands to reason he could change his mind or her mind and -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. So by putting restricted on there, it was your intention that this information not be public but basically kept secret at this point?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kept internal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And what was it that made you decide that this should be -- this information should be restricted?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at the other documents, if they are of this kind, they all carried that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's not my question. My question is: Was what was it that made you decide that this information, this specific information, should be kept secret?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm answering your question again. It isn't based on specific information like the naming of towns. It was a kind of report that I wanted only those people addressed to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My question is why?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because at this stage, it wasn't ready to be part -- we have a hierarchical reporting system which ends up being all the way that content ends up finding its the way -- all the way to the Security Council. The intention is that certain report is not ready for prime time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This was a period of time, was it not, sir, when you were becoming increasingly frustrated?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: With your reports basically being ignored about what was going on in that border area that you were watching?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ignored by the people they addressed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And that was a source of frustration, in fact at one point I think you said that you were seething with anger about that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you think there had been a better chance of these frustrations of yours being answered and relieved if this information which you restricted, you had simply revealed to the public?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because we have a certain reporting responsibilities in an organisation like the UN. You started your testimony here reading a document of the Secretary-General. That is a system followed to inform until the information is vetted and then it goes to the next level. That's the system followed. So if I have information of this kind, I couldn't make it public, nor did I wish it to become public.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You mean you were restricted, you were -- you were prohibited, your job description wouldn't permit you, to make this information public?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have discretion at my level, and working in the UN, to decide which piece of information I would restrict to the person named. I have that discretion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think we will continue this a little bit after we have a break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We will have a 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have the list now, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was handed it right before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So before we continue, again I have another appeal to make on behalf of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I've been severely chastised already by the interpreters, by our Registrar representative. I've got lots of grief during this break, Your Honour. If you want to add to it, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought you looked quite down after the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour at least on this occasion, the Defence and Prosecution get entirely the same treatment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please be considerate with the interpreters, as much as you can. I know that I commit -- I make the same mistake myself and I know it's not easy because one gets carried away as one goes along. So I will try, if perhaps you could draw my attention, either on the monitor or some other way when it gets out of hand and I will try to control the situation as much as I can. Thanks. Mr. Kirudja and Mr. Ackerman, you've heard me, please go ahead, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, before the break we were discussing your memorandum of 3 July, P1671. There came a time after 3 July when that memo was somehow leaked and I take it you have no idea how that happened?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can take it quite correctly. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Was it leaked in your area or was it leaked in New York? Do you know where?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just said no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us about when that information was leaked?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If we can check the note, there is a meeting where this -- subsequent to this memorandum being leaked, where I got a visit from all my bosses, from New York, from Zagreb, all in Topusko, around that date which I don't have, they came to discuss it, subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would that be somewhere in your diaries?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can find that out later but you can say it's about a month or so after this memo was written.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would it have been before all of the press descended on your door step?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, the press and the leaking are part of the same -- that issue of the press descending being on my office was triggered by this memo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
