utterances.text: Do you know that the press got involved in the issue of the camps, made demands to be allowed to go there and visit them, which were allowed, and that by the end of July, both Keraterm and Omarska had been closed. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, they hadn't been closed by the end of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sorry, I got the wrong month.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: By the end of August; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had also very little access to the press other than their presence in my sector. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to you look, then at the last -- the last paragraph of that letter, of that memorandum. We have requested a minibus with driver to help in transporting the escapees to safety and we are talking about these refugees coming across the river basically into your section. Transporting the escapees to safety, since UN vehicles are not to be used for humanitarian purposes. What is that all about?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me a little earlier about the frustration in handling this matter internally. You're now getting deeper into it. That is I have vehicles, military pattern vehicles, deployed around this UNPA, and you have a lot of people in need. The soldiers have certain rules about the vehicles they have. That doesn't include transportation of refugees around. And I was running straight about that and the difficulties, you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. have vehicles parked here, you have refugees in need and you have a bureaucracy to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is this an UN restriction that vehicles under control of UN can't be used for humanitarian purposes?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. Sorry again to the interpreters, I interrupted. There are vehicles designated as military pattern vehicles available to peacekeeping forces. We have a situation where peace wasn't being kept and you can see and draw conclusion as to what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. So I think what you're telling me, correct me if I'm wrong, is that if they have been designated military vehicles, regardless of whether they are minibuses that carry 20 people or not, if they have been designated military vehicles then they can't be used for humanitarian purposes?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are not available.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Wow. Tell me, in your mind, in your own definition, what the difference is between a concentration camp and a detention centre?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all candour, until General Nambiar called me about that, I had not thought about it, but if you ask me now, as opposed to then, I am no better even today in distinguishing the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They are both places where people are kept in a concentrated area, detained in a concentrated area, I take it. That's kind of --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour you have to get somebody else to be definitive about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will, Mr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll leave it alone. July 18th, 1992. I'm continuing with this frustration we are talking about here. On July 18th, 1992, your superiors in Zagreb specifically directed you to not be involved with what was going on in Bosnia, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You'd been sending, as you've said many times, reports alerting them to what you saw as a deteriorating situation in Bosnia and along that border, and you were simply directed by them to ignore that situation. Do you know why?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I have explained in the testimony earlier. They thought we were basically crossing the border, I mean the UN assets deployed in the area, and getting involved, as the testimony shows, since they ignored the reports, they missed the point that they were coming into the centre, into the UNPA. I sought to dispel that misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But did you get the impression that they sort of wanted to -- really didn't want it know what was going on in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would that have been maybe some fear that if they knew what was happening they might have to do something about it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I was trying to get them to do. I have also testified here, we had a withdrawal of the two agencies most responsible for this kind of thing, namely the UNHCR and ICRC. The testimony here shows they had withdrawn. But that wouldn't stop these people in need from coming, and my purpose is to say something needs to be done in the interests, humanitarian interests of these people, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. All of them. And you mean that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. On July 21st, Croatia had agreed to accept 4.000 refugees from Bosanski Novi, correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you look at P1672 now, please? In the document I'm referring to is the second document in that bundle. It's the 6 July, 1992 letter from Radomir Pasic.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And let me just clear up one thing before we go much further. Throughout your reports and your testimony and everything else, you referred to people like Mr. Pasic as mayors. The actual title of these people were presidents of municipalities?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm fully aware of that, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mayor is just a sort of convenient way for those of us who speak English to refer to those municipality presidents that -- it's just a translation issue?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. The -- this letter from Mr. Pasic speaks about a group of people who want to leave and who have been issued permits allowing them to leave, and he requests that you provide safe passage. Right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this in fact happened, and this is the group that grew from an estimated 4.000 up to around 9.000, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it was all done.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When it was all done. And you know, don't you, that many of these people travelled in their own private cars?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we helped them to cross?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We haven't given the details of that testimony. If you like, I can tell you. There were some who -- but a small group -- had their own private cars. The bulk were transported by buses from Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this letter does --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think the documents indicate that there were around 200 private cars involved in the convoy.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you that there were 200 because we also had to supply UNHCR trucks as well as supplementary vehicles so while I said I saw private cars that's true, how many there were, I don't know. 200 right now sounds too much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the trucks were for carrying their personal belongings, was it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The trucks were because we started with 4.000 and then people came in all shapes, and some were just being transported with the trucks, with a bed, only with a mattress on it, truck bed, I mean, with mattresses, and I remember even old people sitting in these truck beds.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: These people took with them, did they not, whatever it was they wanted take that they could, you know, physically transport?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basically, if they were in the car, that wouldn't apply because I wouldn't check, I had no time to check what was in the car. If they were in buses and those trucks, the majority had very bare essentials around.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just going to ask you some things here and you just tell me if you agree, disagree or don't know. These people were not searched for harassed by the Serbian authorities in any way?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And with many of these people, no papers of any kind were required by the Serbian authorities?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not by -- within the transit area, nobody searched them. I can't testify at when they were held at the entry point coming into the sector. Can't testify whether there were papers or what they were doing at the entry point. At the end of the journey, they were received by the Croats. There, they were -- there was an attempt to go through a formal procedure that went on until about 11.00 or 12.00 midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And would it surprise you if one of the Muslim residents of Bosanski Novi had said that they would even have been permitted to take their houses if they could have somehow put them on wheels and taken them along?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If somebody said that, it wouldn't surprise me if you say that someone said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, you were basically opposed to accepting these refugees out of Bosnia, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have testified to that effect in the process of discussing with the Bosanski mayors and Dvor, once they considered to me and the record shows these were not voluntary. At that point, I wasn't in agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In fact you actually tried to persuade UNHCR and ICRC to join your position in that regard, to oppose --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, they joined that opposition, they joined that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Maybe I'm confused. Let me see. In the Milosevic case, your testimony there on 3 February, and this is the source of the question I just asked you, sir. Page 15432. You were asked the following question and gave the following answer: Question: What was your position regarding future similar excavations -- evacuations related to what you believed was ethnic cleansing? Did you support the idea? Answer: No. As a matter of fact, as soon as this -- this matter was clearly understood, both by my headquarters, UNHCR and ICRC, and following that transit by 9.000, we sought to make it clearer to them that this is the beginning. If you allow it, it is going to be a flood and therefore we continuously tried to give them to understand what we knew, and I'm glad to report they did turn around and joined -- I mean they meaning UNHCR, ICRC, they did turn around to our position that this is an affair we couldn't be involved in, correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a correct testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Right. What logic, sir, told you that from a humanitarian perspective, the greater good would be to leave these people in a war zone where they were in grave danger rather than allow them to be transported to safety from which they might one day return? What was the logic in that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a time line in your question, and also implied in the testimony you read from the other case. Not only that we opposed that from happening early in July, but it still happened that instead of 4.000, 9.000 crossed. We had various discussions leading up to the time the first lot left, and during those discussions, this idea that if you do it, you will just open the flood gate was constantly discussed and eventually subscribed to by the humanitarian agencies themselves. But at a certain point during those discussions, a decision was made that is contained in a letter entered in testimony from Prime Minister Greguric, where the Croats who up to a point also agreed with that policy changed their mind and allowed the 4.000. During all that process, the logic was as follows: We are trying to get de-escalation of tensions and fighting. Something the United Nations were called upon to do, basically in the area where we are deployed. These events were happening outside that area, where the United Nations had not read as a war zone in May, at least in May, 1992, and April, when we deployed. So the logic was: Do not -- discourage as much as you can the solution to a conflict that results in displacement of people. That logic is not only local for that time. It's a logic that permits all UN endeavours to stop conflicts and have a local solution than displace people. That logic permits the whole raison d'etre of peacekeeping.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that's the point, isn't it, when you're saying to people stay in a place where the UN is not deployed, where we can't protect you instead of coming to a place where we are deployed where we can. My question is how does that make sense?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That statement you just said, people deployed -- where the UN is not deployed contains a problem. The reason it's not deployed is because it's not a war zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So it's your --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UN is not deployed -- sorry to interrupt, the interpreter, again, so if you -- if you prefix that question to an area where it's a recognised war zone and we are deployed there, I can see what you're getting at. If it isn't an area where the UN is not deployed, it also means there is no reason to be evacuated from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So it's -- it was then your position and that of the UN, that at least up until -- see what you said in Milosevic -- that this 9.000 and this 9.000 we are talking about was the 9.000 that came out in July?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 23rd of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 23rd of July.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Came out around the 23rd of July?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So when you're speaking in Milosevic about this transit by 9.000, that at that point you sought to make it clearer to them, UNHCR, ICRC, that this was a mistake and that they should join you in opposition to these, so at least by this time, this date of 23 July, your position and that of the UN was that there was no armed conflict going on in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually by the beginning of April-May, that's when we realised that -- May, somewhere May, the request came much earlier, the culmination was in July, so what we saw in April and May would lead us to believe in everything that was visible, this is a normal situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In July, 23 July, when these 9.000 are being transported, you are saying to UNHCR, ICRC, please join us in opposing any further transfers.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Correction. The text you read is encapsulated in a time period. I was answering a question covering from July to 19th of August, when a second round was being attempted. So my comment covered the entire period.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, if you're going to break it down to a certain point, then your comment would need to be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not trying to break it down. I'm just trying to put an end date on when you were talking about this. When you say in Milosevic that you were talking with UNHCR and ICRC after this 9.000?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That they should join you, and in context of what you just told the Judges a moment ago, I take it that it's your position that at least up to that point, sometime around the end of July, it's your position that there was no armed conflict occurring in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It wouldn't be correct, because Bosnia is broader than Bosanski Novi. There was armed conflicts in Sarajevo by then. There were armed conflicts elsewhere. So when you say there was no armed -- is it my position in Bosnia, it wouldn't be correct. There were armed conflicts in different parts of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But sir, we are talking about, and we have been talking about, all morning, when we are talking, for instance, about the phone call from Kupresanin, we are talking about people not coming from Bosanski Novi but just through Bosanski Novi, from Prijedor, Sanski Most, Kljuc, all these other locations?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsellor, the people in every one of those discussions, they are localised as to where they are coming from. The 4.000 are not coming from all those places you have named. The 4.000 are coming from Bosanski Novi specifically from Blagaj. So it's not a generalised thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But, you know, we are maybe having some difficulty here. When you talk in Milosevic case, you're talking about those to come after this 9.000?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. And I mentioned to you earlier, do you want me to distinguish that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And those to come after this 9.000. I mean there is some point where Bosanski Novi runs out of Muslims and we are talking about refugees coming out of these other places that Kupresanin talked about in his phone call.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsellor there is not as much confusion as you would seem to want to see. There is statement to the effect we are taking 4.000 from a specific location, that 4.000 turns to 9.000. We continue to discuss after that, after July 23rd, we want more people to come out from the places that you have named, after. The discussions are talking about people coming from Sanski Most. We told you 11.000. After. This is an attempt after the 9.000. From Prijedor, 8.000. After July 23rd. From Dubica -- from Kostajnica, 500. This testimony is specific and in time and in place. Occasionally, I hear you talking about Bosnia in one breath and specifically, no, I'm -- the testimony I have given is specific to -- as to time, as to place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe I have misunderstood the very basic proposition. You were not opposed to refugees coming from Prijedor and Sanski Most and these other places? You were not opposed to having them transit through Sector North?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The testimony is contrary to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. We are back where I thought we were. You said that the reason that you would oppose these transfers had to do with the fact that those people were not living in a war zone, and my only point in the question I was trying to ask you was then it's your position that during that period of time, whatever period of time it is, we are talking about these people coming from Prijedor and places like that, it was your position that there was no armed conflict occurring in those places at the time?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have testified that in the process of finding out who was coming from where, we learned there was a conflict that started at a specific time for the reasons given between the Serbs and Muslims, specifically about not signing allegiance. We have testified there was that kind of conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But that's not a battle, that's not an armed conflict of people shooting at each other?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I think we've exhausted this point, sir. I don't think we can probably take it much further. I'd like you to look at your diary for 12 August, 1992, if you will.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, counsellor, date?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 12 August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 12 August, 1992. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You recorded in your diary -- you were speaking on that date with the mayor -- the municipal president of Bosanski Novi again?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you recorded in your diary a quote from him, and I think it was this: The Serbian side is not respected, there could be massive deaths on both sides. If we are left to resolve the matter by ourselves, we resolve the platter very quickly. For example, there are 7.000 Serb refugees from Croatia in Bosanski Novi. The world did not condemn their plight. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know why there were 7.000 Serb refugees from Croatia in Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was evidence that a lot of movement had taken place prior to our arrival, as a result of the conflict between Croats and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you agree that they were forced out of areas where they had been living for a very long time, by the Croats?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There I face a dilemma. The dilemma being, the area we are deployed on, the United Nations Protected Area, is under total control by Serb authorities. I also testified there was no duress, there was no stress for any Serb crossing that segment of the border where the Serbs were in control of both sides. If they had been displaced from Croatia, this area or their houses, the dilemma for me is to figure out are they Serbs that are choosing to move from other areas or this area where there was a war? If it is this area where there was a war, it also didn't add up to why they would have to run away from an area controlled by Serb forces. That was a dilemma to try to figure out about those 7.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know if any of the Serb refugees who went into Bosnia were assisted in any way by ICRC, UNHCR, the UN, in their efforts to cross into Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At what period? If they left before we arrived, obviously I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. And during the time you were there, were you aware of any such efforts?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not all of which is in testimony because I mentioned -- and this is a point in the other trial, Mr. Milosevic and I engaged with each other for sometime. It's not evident when we helped the Serbs because there was no issue around it. The trucks arrived routinely, humanitarian trucks, loaded with medicine, or other things, in the Serb area, and because the Serbs controlled it, there were no flash points so you don't hear about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. The statement that this municipal president made to the effect that if we are left to resolve the matter by ourselves, we will resolve the matter very quickly, you have no real idea what he meant by that, do you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because at this moment is the point your questioning me about. He did see that we had trouble buying the voluntary removal of Muslims as he proposed, and he was warning us at times saying if you prevent this from happening, if you force this, we will act on our own. That's what he is telling us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were you aware that there were basically two routes, one was to come through your sector into Croatia, and from there elsewhere, the other was to go into central Bosnia over mount Vlasic to Travnik, that direction? Were you aware of those two routes?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The route for what groups?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: For the Muslim people?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was because I was made aware right at the beginning and in the context of asking what's going on and Mayor Pasic said they could have gone through that central Bosnia to Zenica he said but they chose not to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you know that those Muslim people were demanding that they be able to go through Croatia rather than go into central Bosnia primarily because they didn't want to be conscripted into the Bosnian military?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to deconstruct your statement. The part where you say they were demanding that they be able to go through Croatia, not correct. I hadn't met them to make that demand. Serbs were demanding that we let them pass through.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But they were telling you that the Muslim?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Second point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just a minute. The Serbs were telling you that that's what the Muslims were requesting that they wanted to go that direction rather than the other one?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correction. They were telling me actually their words were we have decided, we Serbs, in our generosity to make it easy for them to pass through this safely and you film them passing safely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And one way to resolve the matter very quickly would be for this municipal president to tell those Muslim people who were wanting to leave that they were now down to one choice, and that was to go into central Bosnia, right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sounds to me like you're drawing a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm asking you if you agree with it.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It is the case, is it not, that there were several Serb refugees in Sector North who had fled from Bosnia under the pressure and terror inflicted on them by Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that there were Serbs in Sector North who had come from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You don't agree that they had fled under pressure and terror inflicted on them by Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know any family that was in the sector that came to us and said this is the reason we left. They had no reason -- by the way I don't imply that anything else. I imply that there was no issue about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour I should say this is something we've discussed before. As Your Honours know tu quoque is not a Defence and we've never disputed that there may well have been atrocities against Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Serbs in central Bosnia so Your Honour from that point of view I do ask why this is relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You want an answer, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour I think it's relevant just to show that the whole issue of what was going on in Northern Bosnia, the area just across the border, was fairly complex and not just a simple expulsion of Muslim people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, I think that's not in dispute. I mean no one ever imagined for a moment, since we've started this trial, that the situation was not complex in any of the regions or any of the parts that we have been dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I think that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We have talked about your position regarding your concern about permitting these refugees to come out of Bosnia and go through Croatia, either to remain there or go on to Western Europe or somewhere else. And about your awareness that there were Serb refugees coming from Bosnia into Croatia. But you said that you were not greatly concerned about them because they seemed to be being accommodated, they seemed to be being taken care of, and they did not basically create a refugee problem, correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't become a crisis. They were still refugees, even if they were there, for -- in recognition of which we organised supplies to come into the sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just don't see anywhere in any of your documents sir, where you expressed your opposition to Serbs coming across the border, Serbs being displaced from Bosnia, and coming across the border and becoming refugees in Croatia and perhaps going on elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't see that concern in any of your documents. You have that concern about Muslims but I don't see it about Serbs. Am I there? Am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right, you don't see it. It isn't true what you're implying by it. The testimony I have given constantly is that the UN was not being asked in a crisis situation by the Serbs other than help us we are settled here. This testimony you are referring to is taken by the Prosecution, me answering the questions they are asking me. I don't volunteer them what to ask me. I don't ask them ask me now about the Serbs. If they do, the answer would be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, okay. So are there then in existence reports that are just not included, not attached to your statement, where you were expressing the same kind of concern to the authorities in Zagreb about the movement of Serb people from Bosnia into Croatia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There are?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, correction, not into Croatia. The Croatia is the term you use in this -- with very careful. Croatia is the bigger nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I agree with you. I know what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: So secondly, when I said there are the Serb refugees that we dealt with in almost a crisis, they weren't going to Croatia. They were going into a pocket of Bosnia where the Muslims were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You talked -- you've talked in your materials and in your statements and in your testimony about numerous interviews that were conducted of Muslims coming out of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Did you also conduct the same kind of interviews, similar numbers, with Serb refugees coming out of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Same question you asked earlier. There were already in the houses and quietly -- didn't arise. The issue didn't arise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. So the interest was not so much whether they were in a refugee status or how they got there, it was whether they were making demands on the UN or not?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The issue was you have a person far away from where they live, they are in a hostile area and they are asking for A, protection, and for support. That typical UNHCR issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I guess the difference in your mind between the Serb and Muslim refugees was the Serbs were not a burden and the Muslims were?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's a mischaracterisation, a complete one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This first group of Muslims, as a matter of fact, from Bosanski Novi, the group of 5.000, they were really not asking much of anything from the UN other than safe conduct across Sector North. They asked for no food, no clothing, no nothing, just to get across there, right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just finished testifying, when it actually happened, we had to have trucks there, UNHCR, food there, everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, no, no. You're talking about that 9.000?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm talking about that first group of 5.000, the early group that wanted the television cameras and everything else.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't meet them. I met Serbs talking about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But what they were requesting -- we are not communicating again. What they requested from the UN was only two things: Safe conduct and a television crew.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, you don't hear me. It wasn't the Muslims that were requesting. It was the Serbs who were requesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand. All that was being requested, no matter by whom, was safe conduct and a television crew?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say it was the Serbs that were requesting and not the Muslims, what you're saying is the Serbs were reporting to you that the Muslims voluntarily wanted to leave and they wanted safe conduct and the Serbs wanted it filmed by a television crew?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Look at P1669, if you will, please. The second document there sir is a letter of 20 June, 1992 that we talked about yesterday that was written to Mr. Pasic and we won't discuss the author. In this letter concern is expressed about the welfare of Muslims in President Pasic's community, and he's advised in that letter about the international law regarding population transfers as was understood by you or the author of the letter at that time. The question I have is this: Do you know of any kind of a similar letter expressing the same kind of concern, containing similar language, that was ever sent to the municipality president of Bihac or any of the other Muslim communities in Bosnia regarding the Serb people living in those municipalities and your concern about them?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within our mission or in the entire UN operation? When you say any kind of letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Within your mission. This was within your mission?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, within Sector North.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This letter --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Was there a similar letter that came out of Sector North written by the same person or you or any other person?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Keeping in mind, Mr. Ackerman, because we have to be fair with the witness, that this is not a letter that came from his mission or his office but -- he discussed it with the person who at the end of the day affixed his signature, but this letter did not come from his office. So I think you ought to address the question twofold. His office and if he is aware from any other office.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't wanting to be that specific, Your Honour. This is a letter that he testified yesterday that he had a great deal to do with the contents of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In many ways he drafted it himself and it just went out over the signature of this other person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because it --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because that's how it could be for reasons that he explained yesterday. He was being accused practically of --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All I'm wanting to know, was there a similar letter that he's aware of written by anyone to the Muslim municipalities, expressing the same kind of concern about the Serb people and Serb refugees.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll answer your question. No, there was no letter. Two, there was no similar circumstances that we knew of in the areas you have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you at the time have a position or do you have a position about what the legal ramifications are about forcing people to remain in a place which they are desperately trying to depart? Would that also have been improper and perhaps illegal?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll defer to matters of legalities to Their Excellencies, the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kirudja.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever consider, sir, what the affect might be of forcing people to stay in a place that they wanted to depart?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And indeed, this -- you asked me earlier why the frustration. We had to deal with all of those. Usually long restless nights. If we had any information that people were being hurt, we were duty-bound to evacuate them from where they were. We wouldn't countenance for a minute keeping people where they were being hurt.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This time period we are talking about, basically early 1992, you of course took a definite position about these Muslim refugees that were coming out of Bosnia, that you were -- you disbelieved that they were coming voluntarily, and you were basing your position at that time on the proposition that the Serbs and even some Muslims who you talked to were not being truthful about the desire of Muslims to voluntarily leave the area, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question has several parts. I'll take them one by one. My position that they were coming out of Bosnia, you're wording, disbelieved, my testimony is more than disbelief. I questioned the speaker to the point of admission they were not. They confirmed that. It's not a matter of belief. This is a matter on record them saying, yes, we admit they are being forced. Two, is it that Muslims who were -- you talked to were not being truthful about the desire of Muslims to voluntarily leave the area? The testimony was they were very careful in our presence -- in our presence not to cross or say hard things about their Serbian colleagues. That is the wording. Where we read issues of safety for them before and after the meeting were paramount.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he explained this yesterday, Mr. Ackerman, he drew a distinction yesterday between the reaction of the Muslims under different circumstances when they were faced with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I know, Your Honour, that was basically a preliminary question. I'm now going to where I'm trying to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir I want to talk to you about the meeting you had on 19 August with Vlado Vrkes from Sanski Most. You might find your note on that to maybe assist you in your answers.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 19th of August?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Present at that meeting there was an individual named Besim Islamcevic, who was a Muslim, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us everything you recorded in your notes that Mr. Islamcevic said at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. I told you everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You already did?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He indicated did he not, that he was a representative of the Muslims and Croats willing to leave Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. That was his representation to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know how it happened that that group came to meet with you in the first place?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Say how it happened.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They know where I was. We had already met earlier and they knew my address.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would it surprise you to learn that it was Mr. Islamcevic who requested Mr. Vrkes to set up this meeting with you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. If you say so, I guess it's because you have evidence to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would it surprise to you learn that he asked Mr. Vrkes to set up that meeting because a large group from Sanski Most wanted to leave the area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you don't need to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour it may or may not surprise Mr. Kirudja, it doesn't matter. It's not a proper question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Look at the answer to the first question that you got, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can't follow up with the second question, it's so obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you learn from Mr. Islamcevic at that time that there had been a previous meeting with 28 representatives from the non-Serb community in Sanski Most, in the office of Mr. Vrkes, to express their desires about what it was that was being requested of you in that meeting? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sergio De Mello was present at that meeting, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Was he not?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you recall any question of Mr. Islamcevic as to what would happen if they were not permitted to transit through Sector North?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Summary of what he said to me doesn't include that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you have no independent recollection of that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, it's more than ten years, almost ten years.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand. I'm not giving you a hard time about not remembering. I just want to make sure you don't?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't remember much ten years ago either?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you recall Mr. Islamcevic warning you that their other departure route was very unsafe, via Skender Vakuf and the Vlasic plateau and --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I noted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is uncertain whether or not they reached -- what did you know, tell us?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I noted was something to the effect that all other routes to us are unknown. I remember saying to that you that this man spoke very cautious. He wouldn't have said they were unsafer because I would ask answer from who, so the language he just said was all other routes are unknown. That is in my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Yesterday, during cross-examination about war zones, it was early in my cross-examination of you, page 87, line 13, you said this: The war zone was on the side which was Croatian territory occupied by Serbs. Because I think you thought I was suggesting that the war zone was on both sides of the border and you were trying to clarify that in your view, the war zone was only on the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you referred to the Croatian territory occupied by Serbs. Those are your words. You didn't mean to suggest, did you, that that area, Sector North, had been conquered and then occupied by Serbs during the war with Croatia, did you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsellor, the terminology used in the records you have in front of you would contain no wording to saying occupied. All the documents you have. We are now talking about ten years later. We were not preparing these reports for a court. This Court even as a concept didn't exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir you're misunderstanding me. You're answering a question I didn't ask. Let's see if we can start over?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 87, your answer was this: Precisely, I want something to tell you the war zone was on the side which was Croatian territory occupied by the Serbs. My only question is this: You did not mean to suggest when you used the words "occupied by Serbs" that that had been conquered by Serbs in the Croatian war and then occupied by them. That's wasn't what you meant to suggest, was it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I meant the ordinary meaning that they were there in place and running that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In fact, that is a part of Croatia that was traditionally a very heavily Serb area, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it carried a specific name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In transcript from yesterday, page 32, line 8, Ms. Korner asked you if you ever crossed the bridge into Bosanski Novi, and you replied that you were very careful not to do that because you had been accused of extending UN concerns into Bosnia. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And of course, Bosanski Novi was a Serb majority municipality, right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I remember the numbers, what the proportions were. I'm sure we looked at them at sometime. You can remind me what the proportions are, if you wish to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I don't. My only question is: How many times did you actually cross that border and go into Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The specific question Ms. Korner was with regard to Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand that. I'm asking you about the whole area. How many times did you actually cross the border?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, countless, countless.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You actually had meetings in Bihac, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bihac, Velika Kladusa, and some were inside Blinjski Kut, Bosanski Bojna, all that area, that pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: At some point you learned about the creation of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and learned that it later became Republika Srpska, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I specified the date I learned about Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I can't place a date when I -- when it turned into Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not really asking you for the date. Just that you were aware of that it happened at some point?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You knew, did you not, that the seat of government of this Serbian entity in Bosnia-Herzegovina was in Srpska Sarajevo or Pale?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not or, it was in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at P1669, please. And you'll find a document dated 20 June, authored by Paolo Raffone.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This refers to a meeting that took place in Velika Kladusa with the representative of 850 displaced persons from Sanski Most, correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the report states.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And a representative of this group of displaced persons appeared there, asked that his name be kept anonymous, and then there is a report which follows which Mr. Raffone says is based solely on his statements.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is that another one of the ways that you would say this information is not verified?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly -- well, no, no, no. That is different. That is different. That -- it says what you just read.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to ask you some questions about halfway through that, the third paragraph, he's talking about a -- the sports hall in Sanski Most where people were kept. And he says the guards to this place were under the direction of a man who is the commander of the Serbian crisis committee of Banja Luka, Mr. Davidovic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever make any effort to verify that information?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no reason for me to do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you -- did you ever learn whether that was a true statement or not, that the commander of the Serbian crisis committee in Banja Luka was Mr. Davidovic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no reason for me to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Another thing that this person told you at that time was that with regard to the camp in Manjaca, that it was a camp, it was a place where only dangerous war prisoners, extremists were held, plus some doctors and some members of SDA. True?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is reported speech. My duty was to make sure that we heard what he said and reflected it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And there was not a report from a Serb but from a Muslim --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Representative from Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that information was then passed on, was it not, to higher authorities, to Zagreb and other places?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the letter was actually released by you over your signature?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could you look now at P1671?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Date?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll get there. 8 July.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I may have the date wrong. No. This is not the report I'm interested in. I've got the number wrong. 1672, I'm sorry. This is 8 July of 1992, and this issue of refugees trying to cross from Bosanski Novi has been going on now for quite sometime, more than a month at least, yes?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this report discusses 18 persons who arrived from Bosanski Novi, asking for protection and assistance, to cross Sector North towards Zagreb and other foreign countries, correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And they told stories about persecution, intimidation and deportation going on in Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Question for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah. It's in the second paragraph. They made statements, they told stories, about what they were experiencing in Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Second paragraph, yeah. I see it, the contents of second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Muslims continue to suffer persecution, deportation, intimidation, from Serbian armed groups?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's what they said?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you if you have, outside of your sojourn there in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. former Yugoslavia, in your mission there, do you have any experience with, generally, asylum seekers and what asylum seekers are up to?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, personally.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have worked all my life with the UN and we don't receive asylums.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know just from being a man of the world, that people frequently show up in various countries, usually western countries, seeking asylum?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yeah, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you know that to obtain asylum, they have to have a pretty good story about what's happening to them in the place they came from, why they can't go back?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stands to reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And you know that frequently when those stories are checked out, they turn out to be untrue and they are not granted asylum?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't -- I don't know any story that can verify yes or no to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Right. You did know, and you do know, from what you've read and your experience there, that the economy of Yugoslavia had been deteriorating significantly?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Both before the war and during the war, that there were major economic problems, that inflation was horrible, that life was not what it had been, and that immigration to some western country would have been a desirable matter for anybody living there, correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, I would say that stands to reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And because of that particular situation, in early 1992, that was going on, the situation made it easy for people to make up stories about persecution, become a refugee and gain asylum in some western country, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I focus particularly in your statement, situation made it easy for people to make up stories. Counsellor it's a tall statement. If you see people in dire needs, far away in the conditions I saw them, it would be callous for me to say they were making up stories.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, people could, you know, who are not in that kind of dire situation, and just want to emigrate to some western country, could say, oh, me too, I'm also one of those?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a truism. I will allow that. But as a truism people can make up stories.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You know or do you know that there are tens of thousands of former Yugoslav citizens now living in western countries who left during the war with absolutely no intention of going back there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know some, in New York.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look at -- a little further down through this statement, through this memorandum by Paolo Raffone, the next to the last paragraph, the persons interviewed believe, very last part of that says they are talking about the stadium in Bosanski Novi, when the stadium is full, the guards take some of them away to unknown destinations, some witnesses report that in the first 15 days of May, some 200 persons taken out of the stadium were shot dead nearby. Did you make any effort to confirm that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That they were -- some people taken shot, nearby and shot?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no resources of course to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: To your knowledge, has there ever been any confirmation of that statement?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, no resources that I could put to use. Had this been claimed as happening within the centre, I can tell you I had enough resources to investigate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it doesn't say there right after that, there is no independent confirmation of this report, does it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This again counsellor, it says this is a report based on a person, and other than putting quotes all over his reported speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours and Ms. Korner, I now want to refer the witness to what was attachment number 5 to his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you confused me there. It's 16 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I could not determine if it had ever become an exhibit. I think it might be 165 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. No, no, no. It has become an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 1658, then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, definitely it has. That is the document that was added upon, no? We had two pages only and you had --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's it. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we have 1658 and 1658.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think 1658 is the part that I want --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The 20 May note is what I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 26th of May note?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There is one dated 20 May.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It begins with geographic and ethnic outlook.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour that was the bit that was added.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is 1658.1.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 1658.1. I don't see it in the usher's hands. Doesn't look like mine. Anyway, let's give it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right, sir, you should have a department dated 20 May, 1992, subject note on the situation in Bihac area.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you find that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Who authored that document?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Raffone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Under political analysis, it says this: The representatives of Bihac community explained that their major commercial partner was the Republic of Croatia, nowadays they feel that Croats and Muslims can fight together against the common enemy, the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And so by at least by 20 May, that was the position being taken by these representatives from Bihac, they felt they could join together with the Croats and fight against their common enemy, the Serbs, correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some expressed that view point. I want you to correlate this information of 20th May to testimony elsewhere. We were engaged extensively with demilitarisation and the Serb command was also people we engaged. So you're only looking at one isolated report. The Serb side as commanded by General Spiro Ninkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, let me interrupt you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The only thing I asked you was representatives of the Bihac community said this. I wasn't going beyond this?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm also trying to tell you, you used representatives. This was one representative. I'm serving you notice --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Just a minute, I didn't use representatives. The report uses representatives. Look at the report. The representatives, it uses the plural, not me.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point, he is talking about the people he met that day, who were civil people, civilians. I was referring to the military side which was met, simultaneous, around this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Different subject now. I'm through with that. During the time you spent in Sector North, and referring only to Bosnia, from Bosnia, who were the municipality presidents that you met with and dealt with?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met in Bosnia with representatives of Bihac municipality and Velika Kladusa most often.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You met at some point with the municipal president from Bosanski Novi didn't you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was going to say most often from those of Bihac and Velika Kladusa. And as reported in detailed testimony with those who came from Bosanska Krupa, Bosanski Novi, Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Those with municipal presidents from all three of those places?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's where the testimony in detail comes from. The intention of speaking to you this way, you don't have any details about my meetings in Bihac or Velika Kladusa.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. You spoke of the -- the significant parallel between the positions of the municipal president from Dvor and the one from Bosanski Novi. You spoke of that yesterday. Do you recall speaking of that? I think you used the words it was like they were reading from a script?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, I think it's important for you to explain to the Judges that this Bosanski Dvor area is basically one city divided by a river and a bridge.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Kind of like Minneapolis-St. Paul or some of the --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And until just very recent times and I'm saying recent times in the context of your being there in 1992 --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That river did not form an international border but just a border between Bosnia and Croatia as republics of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And so those two people, those two people who were at that point serving as presidents of those municipalities, were very likely people who had had interactions for many years prior to 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I? Because I don't want to leave that, if you --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I got another question and maybe this will give you a chance to make your speech?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Not a speech, clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: By what you said, you don't propose to make some broad generalisation --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: About what was happening in Bosnia from observing two municipal presidents who were operating within rock-throwing distance?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely why I wanted to clarify. The same analogy which you so eloquently explain between Dvor, applies in Velika Kladusa, Maljevac, and all others, the only difference being while they were on the border, almost Minneapolis-St. Paul analogy, they were not Serb on the other side. So they knew each other and we have testified it was a different picture. Where they were facing, non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'm finished with my questions of you. Thank you very much for bearing with me through this and I hope you have a safe trip home?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsellor I thank you and to the Judges I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] We aren't over with you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You might change your mind. Ms. Korner is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There is, Your Honour but I wonder if we could have the break and then do it because I want to check something over the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, we will have a 25 minute break. I should like to draw the attention of whoever is responsible that there is a discrepancy as to the time that is shown in the transcript, on the monitor and on the LiveNote, and on the laptop. This shows that we are now 12.23 and this shows that we are 12.17. So that might create some problems if one refers to one rather than the other. But I'm drawing the attention of whoever is responsible that there is a discrepancy as to the clock. Okay? 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, you were asked some questions yesterday and the topic was returned to today, in respect of the refugees from Bosanski Novi, that effectively they wanted to leave because of the lack of electricity, the lack of medical care, and the like, and that they were perfectly entitled to want to leave as it was put, voluntarily. I would like you to have a look, please, although you've referred to, at one of the documents in P1669. And if the usher gives it to me, I'll find the relevant document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's the document. It's the document the 8th of June, headed "memorandum" and it comes after the UNPROFOR document. And the subject is the investigative report on the displaced people observed in Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: At the bottom of the page, Mr. Kirudja, you dealt with that meeting on the 27th of May, when the mayor of Bosanski Novi came to see you, and if you turn to the next page, he admitted that the Muslims were not really leaving voluntarily but were under duress?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour this is not proper redirect. This was raised on direct, it was presented on direct. It's not proper redirect at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You put -- you put a specific question to the witness on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, but he testified about this very statement in his direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but let her finish her question and we will be in a position to establish whether it's a proper question on re-examination or not. Had you not brought it up, yes, I would have stopped her immediately, but you put a question and he gave an answer and let's hear your question any way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, in this document, you record the mayor admitted that this was not a voluntary departure by people for -- let's call it globally, economic reasons. Is that your recollection of what he said to you recorded at the time?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In all the massive refugees that were coming through your area from Prijedor, Sanski Most, Bosanska Krupa, did you get any impression from any of them that these people were leaving voluntarily in the proper sense of the word, to escape the economic circumstances or the fact that fighting was going on?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We got the distinct feeling that they were taking a lot of risk both in the route they were taking and where they were going.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think you have answered Ms. Korner's question, Mr. Kirudja. The question was in all the massive refugees that were coming through your area from Prijedor, Sanski Most, Bosanska Krupa did you get any impression from any of them that they were leaving voluntarily in the proper sense of the word to escape the economic circumstances or the fact that fighting was going on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The fact that fighting was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They gave you the impression that they were leaving voluntarily because there was fighting going on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The closest to that statement of choice between economic circumstances or fighting was going on that I'm looking at the monitor, you got the distinct that there were being forced to leave those areas because of conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to come on to the sort of conflict we are talking about, but was this in your view, because Mr. Ackerman asked you a number of questions about asylum seekers, the sort of people who decide there is a better life elsewhere in the sense I can earn more money and the electricity is on the whole time, and that's why I want to leave and become a refugee and try and get into Croatia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't characterise them in that sense like the asylum seekers you see in modern day today in different countries, looking for asylum in that sense, in the sense the counsellor was asking me in that exchange I wouldn't characterise them like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you leave a place because your village has been attacked, you have been dismissed from your job, your family has been split up, and members of your family have been taken to, let's call them detention centres, is that in your understanding of the word a voluntary departure?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's what I said -- I said to understand and I came to the conclusion, as my testimony shows, it wasn't voluntary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you notice, for example, let us take Prijedor, a huge number of Serbs coming through your area from the Prijedor region, leaving because of economic circumstances or the like?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsellor, for Prijedor, we only got notification, in the period following the first departure, that 8.000 would be coming. I underscore they never actually -- that number didn't come from Prijedor. We were just notified by the authorities, you can expect this number from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you understand of what ethnicity or nationality those 8.000 that might be leaving from Prijedor were?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Collectively we only were given to understand they are non-Serbs, not wishing to sign allegiance to a Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What about in relation to Sanski Most? Was that the same?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of these were all characterised as non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you were asked then at one point about whether you had sent a similar letter like the one that was sent by UNHCR to Mr. Pasic explaining that forced transfer or mass transfer of population could be characterised as a crime, and you were asked whether that had been sent, for example, to the mayor of Bihac. I want to ask you a little bit about your knowledge of the events in Bihac. Were you aware that before your arrival in December of 1991, that the SDS had established a separate municipality of Bihac?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you aware that it was effectively divided into two parts, one called Ripac and the other Bihac?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't specifically focused on that division at the beginning. Later on, there was a reason for the division of Bihac but not at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
