utterances.text: Were you aware that in fact the Serbian population of what was then the whole of Bihac had moved over to Ripac so that Bihac was surrounded, as you put it, I think, earlier, by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware that there were in Ripac, as you put it, in that part. But I did -- I knew because at the time we started going to Bihac was a perfectly normal town, not a window broken, everything was okay, and as we moved everywhere, it was clear that there were Serbs and non-Serbs in Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Final question on that, because this is after your arrival. Were you aware in May that all the Muslims who lived on that part of the -- who lived in that part of the area of Bihac which is known generally as Ripac were told to move out and go into the actual Bihac area itself?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wasn't specifically aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In that case, I'll leave it. Thank you. Now, it was put to you that the UN organisations, yourself, UNHCR and also the International Red Cross were in some way behaving badly by not allowing these people to -- the people who voluntarily in inverted commas wanted to leave, to go through into your areas and not giving assistance. I want you to have a look please again at one of the documents, one of your sit-rep reports, please, which is -- it was document 41, which is Exhibit 1684, I'm told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The report of the 8th of October.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you turn into that to paragraph 12? We read part of the paragraph when you looked at it originally.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We dealt with Lord Owen and Mr. Vance in the visit to Banja Luka. The practice of ethnic cleansing appears to continued unabated. Towards the end of July, the UNHCR announced that the UN would in no way Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. participate or do anything that would seem to encourage the practice. Specifically, the UN would not participate in arranging mass relocation of refugees from their houses if the cause of their displacement is the result of ethnic cleansing. And in the last two weeks, this opposition principle appears to have been degraded by -- now, what was it -- well, first of all what is defined by you and the other UN organisations as ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, by this time, as you correctly point out, we had begun to concede that this is indeed what was happening and we used that term guardedly, and I believe it's in quotes, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it is in quotes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To signal we were using it very guardedly. This was where people were moving from their homes by reason of what locally was called nationalities, would you call that ethnicity, and there were always the three groups of Serb, Croat and Muslims. So there was no other reason why this group was being -- was moving except that they were quote non-Serb, not that -- not anything else, at least at that time that was represented to us or told otherwise. The only reason is they are non-Serbs, not wanting to serve allegiance, and that's what we meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In your view, can that be equated with a situation where there is all-out, pitched battles going on, if you like, in which the civilian population is caught in the middle?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it cannot. Bullets and artilleries don't distinguish ethnicities, once the artillery begins to fall in a town, everybody there whether they are one nationality or another are at risk.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, you may misunderstand the question. What you were asked about was effectively conflict all over Bosnia where there was fighting going on and refugees leaving because of, effectively, fighting going on between two sides. In your view is this what you were describing by use of the term ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were describing that systematic identification of a group and then as a result of being identified as non-belonging then you're given terms that force you to leave. That's what we mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, why was it that you or UNHCR announced that you would not assist in any thing that would encourage the practice?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you look into all the testimony, in all those meetings where Pasic and others were there, UNHCR was present with me, and they were assessing the situation directly as well as in conjunction with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, again, Mr. Kirudja, it's me I'm afraid. What I want to know, is what is the principle that led you and UNHCR to say we are not, as it is written here, going to participate or do anything that would seem to encourage the practice?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was like turning on its side -- upside down what refugees are and what UNHCR does. Refugees by definition are people you meet without being involved, displaced from their normal location where they normally live and you need to assist them and offer them protection and shelter. In this situation, this is their home. This is where they live. And you are now being asked as UNHCR to help them move en masse, not individually, en masse, from that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what did you feel was wrong with helping people move en masse from their homes like that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one should be singled for reasons of who they are to be moved. People can be target for things they do, not for things they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Mr. Kirudja. That's all I ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner. There are some questions from the bench, Mr. Kirudja, Judge Janu from the Czech Republic will be putting some questions to you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, on -- at your statement, page 23, but you don't need it, I will bring you to the situation -- you gave us the information that when you were negotiating with the officials, they were quite frequently replaced, and you also said that quite often you had to start all your efforts all over again. Can you clarify for the Chamber, if you recall -- I carry on -- my question is: Were those officials, to your estimation, capable professionals? That's one part of my question. Were those who were replaced moderate or were they radical? I'm asking this question in the connection what you testified or said in your statement in connection with destiny of Mr. Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Janu. In that connection was a sequence of events that occurred when we arrived we found mayors in each of the opstinas that had been part or made to be part of the UN Protection Area. In that connection, the testimony was the only recognised authority in the area was to be -- was to be the mayor, the chief of police, armed lightly. Everybody else, armed forces, had to be demilitarised. And in that connection, we noticed that in the case of Vrginmost, and this mayor understood exactly what the terms were and set about independently to run his opstina. He was quiet and he was basically what you would call a moderate in your terminology, in the sense that he was just the mayor of the town and dealt with the affairs of the Vrginmost opstina. Conversely, there were other mayors, like in Dvor, Petrinja and Vojnic, who gave a lot of speeches specifically of the kind in my testimony I alluded to: We have fought here before you arrived, you, the UN, we the Serbs can no longer live with anybody non-Serb. As long as you don't understand that, we will not have peace here. Those who gave that kind of speeches lasted much longer than those who were not giving and in the specific case you mentioned, Obradovic was killed, assassinated, early in July, in the testimony you can see, just between the headquarters of the UN and where he was coming from. Now, to complete the answer to your question, when those -- when he was killed, there was a chill. A number of mayors were replaced, and all of them began therefore to speak the same language I referred to earlier, complete deference to the headquarters in Knin, which was in itself not allowed under the Vance plan because Vance plan would not have admitted of any over-arching authority over each opstina. So in a way, they all lined up, the mayors, and they began to speak a certain language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: My second question goes to Exhibit P1669, from 20th of June, 1992. There was your request of the request which was done by somebody else but it was -- you were informed or you gave the impulse for this letter and you asked the mayor of Bosanski Novi, Mr. Pasic, to organise the meeting with the representatives of the refugees which were stationed at that time in Blagaj Japra, and the name of this -- of this representatives were Sifet Barjaktarevic and Fikret Hamzagic. I'm interested in the first, especially in the first one, first representative, Sifet. And my question is: Did you meet those persons or somebody from -- or someone else, meet with them? Was this meeting organised? Or -- and the second part of the question, did you learn later on that this representative, Sifet Barjaktarevic, was killed later on?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Janu, I didn't learn, I just learned from you he was killed later. Didn't learn other time. Yes, we -- as soon as I was told by mayor -- the mayor of Dvor that this group wanted to pass through and that it was a matter that was being handled by Mr. Pasic, I requested that we be able to deal directly, to hear firsthand from the groups' representative and these two people did show up to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before we move on, I'm so sorry, just for the purpose of the transcript, the places that Judge Janu were asking about were of course in the Knin side of the border, the RSK. Your Honour I just wanted to make sure the transcript reflected that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: We had it with another witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. Judge Taya would also like to put some questions to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Mr. Kirudja, I have several questions. On page 4 of your statement, 1999, you said it later became apparent that the Serbs inside the UNPAs aspire to be part of what became popularly known as the plan for the Greater Serbia. Apparently inspired from or coordinated in Belgrade. Thus, the only real border they recognised was at the confrontation line with Croatia and once destabilising events in Bosnia began, Serbs dislocated within Bosnia easily relocated into the UNPAs. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Madam, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: And Exhibit P1674, para 6 states about the relocation of Serbs from Bihac and even from Belgrade to UNPAs. My questions are as follows: First one: Approximately how many Serbs relocated from Bosnia-Herzegovina or Serbia to UNPAs during 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The entire 1992 or?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: From April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Until August?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would suggest, Mr. Kirudja, that you restrict it to the period April-August.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The period of my testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, for the reasons outlined earlier, the numbers were never tallied from the Serb side. I took sometime to explain why that was so. So we didn't have the numbers inside for that period. We just knew they were there. We could see some of them. But we didn't make an effort to tally them all up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Did any Serb authority have to do with this relocation?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Evidently, because once you come into the sector, they vetted you, so to speak, who you are, and once you are authenticated to be the person they would allow to be in that sector -- UNPA, they let you be there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: UNPROFOR's mandate were, according to you, firstly, demobilisation, secondly, the restoration of law and order and thirdly helping the return of displaced people, is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Madam with the exception of the second one which I like to clarify. The UNPROFOR itself didn't have the mandate for law and order. UNPROFOR was to monitor law and order, being exercised by the authorities of -- I described, like mayors and chiefs of police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: But to maintain status quo was also UNPROFOR's mandate; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, a very important one. It was maintain the status quo while the political issues that led to the fighting were being negotiated and presumably settled elsewhere, specifically international conference on the former Yugoslavia headed by Stoltenberg on the UN side and Lord Owen on the European side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: So UNPROFOR, according to your statement, I understood that UNPROFOR made every effort to stop expelling Muslims and Croats from UNPAs is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a requirement, a mandate, that whoever was there had to remain there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Then what was the UNPROFOR's stance against the problem of relocation of Serbs?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Problem of UNPROFOR about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: The relocation of Serbs?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was not a problem that I pointed out other than noting that there were Serbs who were native to the UNPA meaning that they always were there, before, during and after the war, and there were other Serbs who had come from elsewhere inside the sector, relatively without a crisis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: But relocation of Serbs did not infringe upon the status quo?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, and again, something we didn't get into. Our job was much more than what the testimony I have given over these three days was. That was my task with the Croatian side. The Croatian side made it repeatedly that it was our duty to prevent these Serbs from coming inside the sector and the Croatian authorities repeatedly mentioned that this non-Serbs who were in the sector needed protection and they made allegations that they were being harassed and so forth. So on the Croatian side, I faced that problem that you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not most of those relocated Serbs were expelled from the territory of Croatia when Croatia had regained the area of UNPAs?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, I was at that time posted in Belgrade, when the last military action was taken by the Croatian authorities, and I was witness to the long convoy of Serbs arriving through the highway into Belgrade and beyond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Another series of questions is concerning on page 6 of your statement, 2002. On page 6 of that statement, you said, in mid-1993, there were a number of meetings that I attended to facilitate the negotiations with the Croats regarding autonomy for the Serbs in the Krajina. While Martic was clearly involved in these meetings, behind the scenes the Croats would not negotiate with anyone who was a government official in the Krajina. I therefore met frequently with those who were nominated to do the negotiating in these pre-negotiation meetings. It is my understanding that these negotiations broke down a number of times because Martic would sabotage them to avoid reaching an agreement with the Croats, which did not advance his vision of a Republic of Serbian Krajina unified with Serbia. My question is as follows: Did you have any impression that not only Martic but also Tudjman was sabotaging negotiations to avoid reaching an agreement on the subject of autonomy of Serbs in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, this concept of autonomy for the area you referred to as Krajina was a contentious issue, but at certain point, the Croatians were -- didn't want to participate in a manner that would lead to further independence for the area. So you are right, the government of Tudjman wasn't always ready and willing but they did come around and -- under the terms of that negotiation that there would be an autonomy. That in principle they had accepted. What was at issue is the extent of that autonomy and the terms of that autonomy in the context of other UN resolutions. That was what was being negotiated. On the Martic side you referred to the fact that they -- we would come to a point of an agreement and suddenly, everything will break down, and that too happened a number of times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Didn't you think that Tudjman was opposing autonomy because he predicted that Croatia would be able to regain the area of UNPAs while the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina will be escalating?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot rule out that at some point he reached that conclusion. I don't know when he reached that conclusion but I can't rule out that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: But according to you, what were there behind Tudjman's attitude?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in a position, Madam, to give you any details on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have one, maybe two questions depending on your answer to the first question. How long or until when did your assignment in the territory of ex-Yugoslavia last?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire period?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From April, 1992, just about June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I do have a second question to you, and my second question is: Did the events that happened after August, 1992, in any of the areas that you were responsible for, and that is until your departure from the territory of ex-Yugoslavia enable you to in any way look with hindsight at the events that took place between April and August, 1992? And if so, which would be these events? That's the first part of the question.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do have -- like when you are out of a situation, of course, the luxury of hindsight about a number of things. I don't know all the ones that come to mind or in any specific order but because of the testimony I had given earlier one event didn't come up because of -- in the course of that, and I looked at it in hindsight. And that was if the United Nations had successfully implemented the Vance plan, there were opportunities for stopping the cascade of events that led to war extending also in Bosnia-Herzegovina, something I said at the earlier testimony, the UN had assumed that Bosnia-Herzegovina will remain peaceful to the extent of planning to locate our headquarters there. The specific point I had in mind was we had gone as far as the Vance plan requested to convincing the Serbs to put their weapons, decommission them, if you like, into the so-called double key, and let the status quo hold. It lasted oh, I'm not sure of the dates exactly but later than August. By January, 1993, the Croatian side took the first of many measures that later would culminate with the last military action Judge Taya -- the lady on the right side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Taya.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judge Taya. That resulted in that last event. And that was the attack on the bridge called Maslenica that joins the north and south Dalmatia. As a result of that action, the Serbs overran all the depots containing all the weapons and took them all out and they never went back again into storage, nor did they permit the UN to so to speak repair that bridge because in a peacekeeping mission, if you have seen it not only in former Yugoslavia, elsewhere, the name of the game is very often to have one side or the other violate the terms of the cease-fire and for the UN to work to restore that breach. We never got the chance to repair that breach. And then later on, more action took place culminating to the other one. Had that happened, had the Serbs not also taken these weapons, claiming that they needed them for self defence, a point we discussed a lot in the other meeting, in the other testimony, had they said to the UN now hold the other party responsible for violating this and the return, in retrospect, maybe I'm overly optimistic, in retrospect we might have gone into the system of holding until a political solution was found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. In these -- in the course of these last few days, Mr. Kirudja, you've been presented with a series of documents, some signed by you, some signed by others but released by you, and others prepared, drafted and signed by others with which -- with or with whom you had absolutely nothing to do. They more or less present a variety, a number of events and situations which you stand -- which you stood by in the course of your testimony. Do you think, or do you believe, that the events that took place after August, 1992, would strengthen your assessment or the assessment made by others in those documents or would you leave room for a reassessment of the events and the situations that they describe and refer to?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES KIRUDJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes one doesn't even take pride to be proven right. In many of the things what we were afraid would happen did happen, in the sense that the events that followed after that went certain direction. My -- many of my situation reports which dared project, ended up unfortunately being right in the sense that what we were afraid of would happen, happened. You also mentioned there were other reports by other people. There were two kinds in this testimony, at least that I have seen. Those which were people -- by people who reported to me, for which I can speak a lot more confidently and there were a few others, at least in yesterday's testimony that I had seen for the first time. What I concluded from this last category of reports it was a pleasant surprise that they corroborated what we were seeing rather than made it look like we were totally in the dark about what we thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Mr. Kirudja, and that brings us to the end of your testimony here. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, Judge Janu and Judge Taya, the lady on the right as you put it, I should like to thank you for having accepted to come over one second time, one more time, to this Tribunal here in The Hague to give evidence. And I join Mr. Ackerman in wishing you a safe journey back home. The usher will accompany you and you will receive all the assistance you require to -- for the purposes of your return. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Thank to you the counsellors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner, there is a slight problem which may not be slight after all, that I -- my attention has been drawn to. And it relates to the list that you circulated earlier on today, and which Mr. Ackerman was very anxious -- you could see it in his face -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. awaiting -- waiting for. I noticed that in the first part of the document --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is a name and a witness which I am informed comes from or belongs to the Banja Luka chapter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour I wonder if we could go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Let's go into private session.
